name: Japanese Anime Drama Studio
description: Suited to creating Japanese realistic anime style drama shorts, covering themes such as youthful romance, urban light and shadow, missed chances and reunions, and supporting high-density dialogue shorts in multiple language styles such as English, Vietnamese and Japanese.

planning.planning_notes:
[Stage path]
1. Before starting, judge the entry point from total_duration, language_style, delivery_resolution, series_mode, the user input and the canvas/uploaded assets, and lock the global creative specification at the Skill level: 16:9 landscape, 24fps timeline, Japanese realistic anime youthful light and shadow, no BGM, no subtitles, core emotion, target duration, delivery resolution and whether it is a short drama series; this specification creates no standalone node. The total length supports 10 seconds to 10 minutes, with non-preset durations following the user's specification; a single shot is limited by the video generation node's duration cap, and is planned at 7-15 seconds by default. The language and accent style must be asked about proactively; after completing "story direction and language style", a reviewable global specification is formed.
2. Parse the user's inspiration, script and reference material into a story script: when there is only a one-line idea, expand it into a short film script and mark it "auto-expanded, pending verification"; when a complete script exists, parse it faithfully without rewriting the core plot on your own; when there is no story input at all, first ask the user for an inspiration, synopsis or script. Make this stage's output clear and reviewable.
3. Images, videos, audio and documents provided by the user first undergo asset analysis, without creating a standalone node: extract identity features, clothing, micro-expressions, materials, spatial layout, character positions, prop positions, key light direction, color temperature, shadow reflections, continuable camera positions and action end states; if the user designates a piece of audio or video as a voice reference, mark which characters or shots it can bind to, for voice timbre, lip-sync, tone or rhythm reference, and output cross-shot continuity clues.
4. After the script is complete, enter the storyboard stage: establish key_element, the character identity sheets, the scene sheets and the shots in order. Submit the scene sheets after the character identity sheets are complete, and the complete storyboard and shot continuity table after the scene sheets are complete.
5. After the storyboard is complete, enter the key element stage: first list from the key_element entries in the storyboard the independent assets that need to be reused across shots, and create a separate draft node for each asset. Each recurring character is its own node, generating a four-panel character identity sheet; each main reused scene is its own node, generating three kinds of reference images: front / aerial / detail; each core prop, vehicle or environment object that needs a consistent appearance across shots is its own node. Register and bind the user's existing visual assets first; visual assets the user has explicitly chosen and that are directly usable are not regenerated. Do not create just one generic "key elements" node, and do not merge multiple independently referenceable characters, scenes or props into one overview image; only assets that are always referenced downstream as one whole may share a node. Make each key element output clear and reviewable.
6. After the key elements are complete, generate final_shot: first generate one sample that best represents the characters, lighting, camera movement and dialogue rhythm; after the sample is complete and meets the locked requirements, batch-generate the remaining final_shots. Each shot is 7-15 seconds, with no more than 9 reference images and no more than 3 audio references totaling less than 15 seconds; character, scene, prop, previous-shot video or user-designated voice reference assets may be connected, with the supported types, counts and duration limits following the model and generation mode selected on the current node. Dialogue, breathing, action sounds and single-shot ambient sound are written into the corresponding video prompt by default; only when the user designates an uploaded or on-canvas audio/video as a voice reference is @audioN or @videoN used in the video prompt, in the order of the materials connected to the current node, to explain its voice, lip-sync, tone or rhythm purpose.
7. After all shots are complete, final assembly, mixing, 4K upscaling and export are handled by the canvas compose node. When 4K delivery is chosen, finish the 1080p final cut first and then upscale, and make the upscaled final cut clear and reviewable.

[Planning rules]
Every node should preserve room for the user to review and adjust: the character sheets, scene sheets, storyboard table, sample and final cut should all support modification, regeneration or skipping; the storyboard stage can also designate a single shot or adjust rhythm/duration.
When a single generation attempt does not match the confirmed character, scene, shot or continuity requirements, retry once on the same path; if it still does not match, explain the deviation, and do not silently downgrade to a weaker path.
If three consecutive rounds of revision still fail, submit three explicit creative directions instead of repeatedly generating along the same direction.
The locked duration, language and accent style, delivery resolution, episode format and visual specification must run through the script, storyboard, key element and video stages.
By default 2-3 element scenes and at most 4 element characters; these are upper-limit hints on the number of independent key element nodes, not a reason to merge several elements into one node. A short drama series must also lock the character appearance, scene prop positions, lighting state and the purpose of the chosen voice reference assets, so that the end of one episode connects naturally to the beginning of the next.
planning.prompt_guide:
All stage outputs use Markdown in the same language as the user's input, and all downstream prompts are written in that language, unless the user explicitly requests another language.

[Visual language]
Japanese realistic anime, translucent high-saturation colors, golden dusk backlight, a sky gradient from blue-violet to orange-gold, glass raindrop reflections, volumetric clouds and delicate environmental detail. Characters keep a translucent Japanese realistic anime texture: 2-3 star-point eye highlights, semi-transparent grouped hair strands in backlight, restrained periocular and lip texture that appears with expression, natural warm-cool skin tone transitions, and visible hand joints and clothing materials. Keep a delicate sense of life but never turn into a real-person photo, over-smoothed skin, plastic skin, flat shading or unsourced outer glow. Do not directly use specific film/TV works, directors or character names as style instructions; use executable picture descriptions instead; describe only what is visible or audible in the shot.

[Light and shadow and visual motifs]
Every light must have a visible or inferable physical source; the key light direction stays coherent across adjacent shots, shadows keep material detail, and highlights keep texture. Across the whole film, adopt at least three among crossing trams, raindrops on glass, dusk backlight, starry sky, sea of clouds and city rooftops, and land visible details such as rail perspective, raindrop trails with background blur, elongated shadows or a clear Milky Way. Give trams, raindrops, shadows, rails, clouds or the Milky Way concrete spatial relationships and physical causes, rather than piling up visual nouns.

[Prompt organization]
Key_element image prompts are organized as identity and appearance → pose/composition → environment or white background → physical light source and direction → light color → texture constraints.
Scene image prompts are organized as space and narrative props → relative positions of characters/props → time and weather → key light direction and color temperature → shadows/sky/reflections and material detail → composition.
The final_shot prompt is written as compact paragraphs in order of occurrence: connected reference assets and their purpose → starting picture state → shot scale / angle offset / composition → handheld breathing feel and camera movement with acceleration/deceleration → character action, eye line and micro-expressions → lighting and environment changes → dialogue, breathing, action sounds and ambient sound → end state and handoff to the next shot; use @imageN, @videoN, @audioN to point at the reference thumbnails connected to the current node and state the purpose of each reference; do not invent references for material types that are not connected. When the user specifies no voice reference, do not invent @audioN or treat an unrelated video as a voice reference. Reference capabilities and limits follow the model and generation mode selected on the current node, and add "no music, no subtitles, no on-screen text".

[Dialogue expression]
The dialogue language style follows the language and accent style locked at the start: English and Vietnamese use a natural spoken feel, with a few colloquial particles suited to the language; Japanese is written in Japanese spoken rhythm and pause habits. Harsh words are delivered calmly, slowly and held back; require each word to be clear, sentence endings complete and key words stressed, with speaking speed and pauses determined by emotions such as slow, restrained, questioning, sad, bursting or gentle, avoiding swallowed sounds and stiff splicing. The dialogue strictly corresponds to the lip movement. If the user designates an uploaded or on-canvas audio/video as a voice reference, then when generating the video prompt, use @audioN or @videoN, in the order of the reference materials connected to the current node, to explain its voice timbre, lip-sync, tone or rhythm purpose; when no voice reference is designated, write the dialogue performance and sound intent directly in the video prompt.
conduct_rules: Create the complete workflow draft first; the story script, character sheets, scene sheets, storyboard table, sample and batch videos must each have a clear stage output, and the actual pace of continuing, retrying and executing is controlled by the canvas workflow.

dependency_for only controls execution order, and the target node does not consume the upstream output. Story script to storyboard must use context_for; storyboard text to image or video nodes must use prompt_for; visual assets to video nodes must use media_input_for. dependency_for is allowed only when the target does not consume the source output.
The language and accent style must be proactively asked of the user at the start (English / Vietnamese / Japanese), and once locked it runs through all dialogue writing and performance direction.
Default 16:9 landscape, 24fps timeline; the total length supports 10 seconds to 10 minutes, and a single shot defaults to 7-15 seconds, limited by the video generation node's duration cap.

Submit the scene sheets after the character identity sheets are complete, and the complete storyboard and shot continuity table after the scene sheets are complete; do not skip steps or scramble the dependency order.
No shot may be completely static for more than 1.5 seconds; close-ups keep a restrained handheld breathing feel, and establishing shots must have a slow lateral move, tilt or in-environment motion.

Each short uses at least 4 camera angles, with shot scales forming a progression or reverse progression of long shot, full shot, medium shot, close-up and extreme close-up; a front-facing character shot must be offset by at least 15 degrees, and adjacent shots must not repeat the camera position or shot scale.

Avoid angle-less frontal static shots, unmotivated medium shots, mechanical constant-speed push/pull and overly smooth stabilizer trajectories; rapid pushes and pulls must contain a slight inertial overshoot, and pushes, pulls, follow shots and orbits must all state organic acceleration and deceleration.

A continuity table must be established for adjacent shots: the 30-degree rule, action match, eyeline match, screen direction, character position in frame, prop state, key light direction and color temperature continuity, with the duration difference between adjacent shots in the same scene in principle not exceeding 3 seconds.

The performance must write, in visible order, micro-reactions before speaking such as a change of gaze, breathing, swallowing or looking away, then the action, lip movement and wrap-up; emotions are restrained but clear, and shouting, uncontrolled crying, smashing and exaggerated slapstick are forbidden.

Dialogue is written within the corresponding shot, by default one effective line every 3-5 seconds, with each line annotated with the speaking element character, the emotion, the performance rhythm and the stressed words.

Do not design music, cross-shot BGM audio_layers or subtitles; ambient sounds such as rain, tram, cicadas and wind are written into the sound intent of the relevant shots, and an audio_layer with its coverage range and volume level is created only for ambient noise floor that truly must continue across shots, and it must not mask dialogue.

First register and bind the user's uploaded or existing characters, scenes and props to the corresponding key_element or shot; visual assets the user has explicitly chosen and that are directly usable are not regenerated, and a series project keeps reusing the same character, scene and prop states.

The key element stage must not create just one generic "key elements" node. Every recurring character, every main reused scene, and every core prop/vehicle/environment object that needs a consistent appearance across shots must be its own node; do not replace multiple independent elements with one overview image.

No standalone audio node is created by default; dialogue, breathing, action sounds and single-shot ambient sound are written into the corresponding video prompt. Only when the user designates an uploaded or on-canvas audio/video as a voice reference is that material connected to the corresponding video node, and @audioN or @videoN is used in the video prompt to explain the voice, lip-sync, tone or rhythm purpose.

Each shot references no more than 9 images and no more than 3 audio clips totaling less than 15 seconds; only when action match, screen direction, picture state or lighting must be continuous is the previous final_shot's short video additionally referenced, to avoid character and scene drift.
First generate one representative sample, and batch-generate the remaining final_shots only after the sample is complete and meets the locked requirements.

When generation fails or does not meet the confirmed requirements, first retry once with the same configuration; if it still fails, explain the deviation and keep room for adjustment, and never silently switch the voice mode or downgrade to a path that does not match the user's choice.
Video generation does not output 4K directly; 4K delivery must be upscaled after the 1080p final cut is complete, without re-enlarging resources that already reach the target resolution.
Final editing, mixing, upscaling and export are handled by the canvas compose node.

rating_bands.description: The stages are clearly separated with complete stage boundaries, and the Japanese realistic anime texture, physical light and shadow, multi-camera shot storytelling, cross-shot continuity, restrained performance and word-by-word dialogue all land stably in the outputs, with no BGM and no subtitles in the whole film.
The flow is basically complete, but some stages lack asset analysis, asset binding, the continuity table, camera-position diversity, performance micro-reactions or audio node timbre parameters.

Stage boundaries are muddled, a real-photo feel or flat-shaded texture appears, a shot is completely static for a long time, a light has no physical source, or BGM, subtitles or on-screen text are added.

visual_review_items.name: Japanese realistic anime texture
visual_review_items.description: Characters need star-point eye highlights, semi-transparent grouped hair strands in backlight, restrained periocular and lip texture, natural warm-cool skin tone transitions, and visible hand joints and clothing materials; they must not look like real-person photos, over-smoothed plastic skin or flat shading.

visual_review_items.name: Physical light and shadow and visual motifs
visual_review_items.description: Every light has a visible or inferable source, shadows keep material and highlights keep texture, and concrete details of at least three motif types among trams, raindrops on glass, dusk backlight, starry sky, sea of clouds or rooftops are landed.

visual_review_items.name: Cross-shot continuity
visual_review_items.description: Character appearance, clothing, prop state, spatial positions, screen direction, key light direction and color temperature stay continuous across adjacent shots and the whole film.

visual_review_items.name: Diversity of shot language
visual_review_items.description: At least 4 camera angles, shot-scale progression, front-facing shots offset by 15 degrees, handheld breathing feel and organic acceleration/deceleration, with no completely static picture longer than 1.5 seconds.

text_review_items.name: Stage boundaries and adjustability
text_review_items.description: The character sheets, scene sheets, storyboard table, sample and final cut all have clear outputs, input dependencies and room for adjustment, making it easy to review and advance the canvas workflow.

text_review_items.name: Executability of the storyboard and continuity table
text_review_items.description: Every shot has complete fields, including referenced elements, emotional motivation, start/end picture state, shot scale, camera angle, camera movement, key light direction, sound intent and continuity basis, with an adjacent-shot continuity table attached.

text_review_items.name: Dialogue and performance direction
text_review_items.description: Line density, language and accent style, emotion, speaking speed and pauses, stressed words and the order of micro-reactions are clear and correspond to the lip movement.

domain_constraints: Fixed 16:9 landscape, 24fps timeline; total length 10 seconds to 10 minutes, single shot 7-15 seconds by default.
No BGM, no subtitles and no on-screen text in the whole film; this Skill has no narration by default.
The dialogue language and accent style follow the English, Vietnamese or Japanese locked at the start.
Characters must keep the Japanese realistic anime texture, and real-person photo feel, over-smoothing, plastic skin, flat shading and unsourced outer glow are forbidden.
Every light must have a visible or inferable physical source; uniform ambient light, crushed blacks, blown whites and effect halos detached from the light source are forbidden.
No shot may be completely static for more than 1.5 seconds, and the whole film uses at least 4 camera angles.
Each shot references no more than 9 images and no more than 3 audio clips totaling less than 15 seconds.
The final_shot prompt, including placeholders, must not exceed 2300 characters.
Do not directly use specific film/TV works, directors or character names as style instructions.
